paragraphs: The means by which one refutes the claim that God is a body, the doctrine of tashbīh (anthropomorphic likeness), and the assertion of the licit-ness of ruʾya (visual perception of God) — is reason (al-maʿqūl), and reason alone. For the prophetic books, though they contain passages that deny tashbīh in several places, also contain passages that seem to affirm it. Since these two cannot both stand without contradiction, and since the Book cannot contradict itself, it follows necessarily that one of them is true in its plain reading and the other must be interpreted otherwise than its plain sense. What discriminates between the two — what tells us which is to be read as plain and which is to be read by taʾwīl — is reason, which (as we have established above) is the measure of all things and the judge of all things. In our refutation here we do not target the Rabbanites exclusively — for some of them are aware of al-maʿqūl and have not departed entirely from its method. We target all the corporealists (al-mujassima) and likeners (al-mushabbiha) among them and outside our community.[{2}]

What needs to be presented against the corporealists: ask them — on what basis do you claim that the Maker is a body? Their answer is: since we have not observed an active agent except as a body that is alive, and since God is an active agent who is alive — therefore He must be a body. We reply: well, then, say also that He is long, broad, deep, divisible, and capable of being halved — for you have not observed an active living agent except as such. Likewise: say He is composite — for you have not observed an active living agent except as composite. If they try to distinguish — they overturn their own inference. For whoever distinguishes between two cases whose cause is one has overturned his own causal premise. Tell them also: say that places contain Him and touch Him, that He moves and rests — for you have not found a living agent except so.

If they invert the argument upon us and ask: what is your proof that God is a thing at all? — we reply: our proof is that He is affirmed (muthbat). For action is impossible from a non-existent essence; and in language and discourse, negation and affirmation operate on things. When the affirmer says "everything is created" or "everything perishes save God," or "everything is either body, accident, or substance" — and when the negator says "you have nothing of mine," or "there is nothing in the house" — the operation is on thing-hood. Since God (mighty and exalted) is affirmed in existence, He must be a thing. They have no parallel argument for body-hood: people do not use the term body in negation and affirmation in this way. No one says "there is no body of mine with you" or "there is no body in the house," nor does anyone say "every body perishes save God." So our proof that God is a thing is sound; theirs that God is a body is not parallel.

If they say: what is your proof that He is alive? We reply: our proof is the variation (ikhtilāf) of His acts. Varied acts are impossible from anything other than a living, powerful, choice-making agent. Since God is an agent of choice, He must be alive and able. If they say: but action is impossible from what is not a body, just as it is impossible from what is not able — say to them: the situation is not parallel. […] [the recoverable sense is:] the inference from variation-of-acts to living-and-able is direct; the inference from variation-of-acts to bodily is not direct, since the inference applies to agent, and agent need not be embodied.

We can grant for the sake of argument that we have not in fact observed any agent except a body — and the conclusion still does not follow. For: when the contingency of bodies has indicated the existence of an agent for them, we then ask: is that agent a body or not? The argument moves from the existence of bodies to the existence of an agent; once the agent is established, we then ask whether the agent is itself a body — and judge according to evidence. Every body, in immediate rational understanding, is such that it can come into contact with other bodies at some place — otherwise it would not be a body, since it is long, broad, deep, and has a boundary. […] If they say: "by 'body' we mean only existing, not body in the proper sense" — reply: why did you posit this term then? You answered us only that He cannot be existing-and-affirmed except as a body! Were a claimant to say: "the Wise One is a human, because I have only observed a wise being as a human, and by 'human' I only mean affirmed-existence" — would he be right? If they reply: we have observed existents other than bodies — substances and accidents — then we too have observed existents that are not bodies.

What further refutes their entire argument and their school: tell them — why have you claimed that you have not observed an agent except as a body? Have you in fact observed that the body in the observable is, of necessity, the agent? Or do you not know that people have disagreed about the nature of the agent of choice in the observable: whether it is the body, or the soul, or some incorporeal capacity, or neither — and have advanced proofs for their various positions. From where do you presume that you have only observed body as agent? The matter is finally this. Bodies we know by sense; that something is a body, we know directly. But that something is living, we know only by the appearance of its actions — this is not a sense-given property. So being-a-body is not a constitutive property of being-living-and-acting; we move from the action to the inference that this thing is alive and able, and then we inquire whether it is a body or not. The two questions are separable. The corporealist's argument confuses the two by treating "being-alive" as if it were given in the same way as "being-a-body" — but it is not. There is much more we have said on this in other places; this place will not bear repeating; what we have said suffices for one who reflects. ---
